opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question I get a lot, because there's a common assumption that as frontier models get better, the case for adapting open models just disappears. I actually think it's the opposite in many ways.

Frontier models are incredible generalists. But enterprises don't live in the general case. They have their own data, their own workflows, their own vocabulary, their own definition of what a "good" answer looks like. A model that's brilliant at everything on average isn't necessarily the best model for your specific claims-processing pipeline or your internal codebase or your customer support tickets. That last mile of performance is where a lot of the business value actually sits.

There are also very practical constraints. A lot of companies can't or don't want to send sensitive data to a third-party API. They care about latency and cost at scale. If you're running millions of calls a day, a smaller open model that's been specialized for your task can be dramatically cheaper and faster, and often just as good or better on that narrow task. And there's control: you own the weights, you're not subject to a provider deprecating a model version or changing behavior underneath you.

What I think is changing is *how* you adapt. A few years ago, fine-tuning meant you needed a big labeled dataset and an ML team. Now the frontier models themselves become part of the toolkit. You can use them to generate synthetic data, to curate and filter data, to act as judges or graders, and then distill that capability into a smaller open model that you own. So the frontier models getting better actually makes adaptation *easier* and more powerful, not obsolete.

The other piece is that the real bottleneck is rarely the model now. It's the data and the evaluation. Most enterprises don't have a clear way to measure whether a model is doing well on their task. So a big part of the work is helping teams define what success looks like, build good evals, and then build a feedback loop where the model keeps improving as it sees more real usage. That's where I think the interesting work is going to be for the next several years: not choosing between frontier and open, but building systems where they work together and the enterprise ends up with something that's genuinely tailored to them.

r001.rationale: The response says enterprises have their own data, workflows, and vocabulary, and that a generalist model may not be best for specific tasks. It does not clearly identify those tasks as out of distribution for frontier models.

r002.rationale: The response does not claim that frontier improvement alone cannot improve enterprise-task performance. It instead says stronger frontier models can help generate data and distill capability into specialized models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So this is a question I get a lot, and I think the framing people usually bring to it is a little off. The assumption is that it's a race, right? Frontier models get better, and at some point the gap closes and nobody needs to fine-tune anything anymore. And I just don't think that's how enterprise actually works.

Here's the thing. When I was at Google working on recommendation systems, the models we deployed were never the biggest or the most general. They were the ones that were tuned to the specific signals, the specific data, the specific constraints of the product. And the enterprise world has that same shape. Every company has their own vocabulary, their own documents, their own edge cases, their own definition of what "good" looks like. A frontier model doesn't know that your internal ticketing system has three different fields that all mean "priority" and that only one of them is actually correct.

So what we've seen building Bespoke Labs is that frontier models raise the ceiling, but they don't remove the need for specialization. If anything they make it more tractable. You can use a strong model to generate and curate training data, to grade outputs, to act as the teacher. And then you distill that into a smaller open model that you actually own, that runs inside your VPC, that costs a fraction per token, and that you can keep improving as your data changes.

And that last part is really the point. Adaptation isn't a one-time event. The companies that are doing this well treat it like a loop. They log what the model does in production, they figure out where it fails, they turn those failures into data, and they retrain. That's a data engineering problem more than a modeling problem, honestly. The hard part is building the pipelines and the evals, not picking the base model.

I'd also say there's a practical reality around cost and latency and control. If you're running millions of calls a day on a narrow task, a seven or eight billion parameter model that's been tuned for that task will beat a frontier API on cost by an order of magnitude and often match or beat it on quality for that narrow slice. And you're not exposed to a provider changing the model under you or changing the pricing.

So where do I see it going? I think frontier models become the teachers and the fallbacks, and adapted open models become the workhorses. The skill that matters for enterprises isn't fine-tuning as a technique. It's being able to turn your own operational data into a feedback signal reliably. That's durable, and it gets more valuable as the base models improve, not less.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier models do not know each enterprise’s internal vocabulary, documents, edge cases, or correct ticket fields, identifying internal enterprise specifics as outside their existing knowledge.

r002.rationale: It says frontier models raise the ceiling and make specialization more tractable, but does not claim that continued frontier-model improvement alone cannot improve performance on enterprise-internal tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is, what does the enterprise need that the model doesn’t already provide? As frontier models improve, some of the things you previously needed to fine-tune for may work out of the box. So you have to keep reevaluating where adaptation actually adds value.

But a more capable model doesn’t automatically understand your internal terminology, have access to your proprietary information, or fit your deployment constraints. There’s still work to do around connecting it to the right data, evaluating it on your tasks, and making it reliable within your workflows. Fine-tuning is one tool there, but it’s not always the first tool you need.

Open-source models give enterprises more control over that process. If you have a fairly well-defined task, adapting a smaller model can make sense for cost, latency, or where the data needs to stay. The goal isn’t necessarily to beat the frontier model across everything. It’s to meet the requirements of that particular application. As the frontier advances, I think that balance will keep shifting.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier models may lack internal terminology or proprietary information, but does not clearly characterize enterprise-internal tasks as out of distribution.

r002.rationale: It says frontier improvements can make some previously needed fine-tuning work out of the box. It does not claim that continued improvement alone cannot improve performance on enterprise-internal tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think frontier models improving actually makes this question more interesting. The question for an enterprise is, how do you turn that capability into something that works reliably for your particular use case?

A lot of that work is about context: the terminology your organization uses, the information the model needs, the tools it can access, and what a good answer looks like. Adapting an open-source model can give you more control over those things, along with deployment, latency, and cost. But you need to evaluate whether that adaptation actually helps. Sometimes retrieval is sufficient; sometimes fine-tuning makes sense; sometimes a frontier model is the best choice.

So I see this as a moving boundary. As the underlying models improve, some customization becomes unnecessary. But enterprises still need to define the task, build good evaluations, and integrate the model into their workflows. That work remains valuable regardless of which model is underneath.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tailoring models to enterprise use cases, but does not identify enterprise-internal tasks as out of distribution for frontier models.
